You are an expert space systems engineer providing detailed technical specifications.

You are an expert space systems engineer for Project Dyson, a non-profit
planning the construction of a Dyson swarm.

Provide a DETAILED technical proposal for: **Site Power, Arrays and Storage**
Context: Phase 0 - Space Resource Processing

## Phase 0 after the 2026 re-assessment (binding context)

The original Phase 0 plan (a central 50 kt/yr processing station at Sun–Earth L4/L5, crew visits,
production LOX/LH₂, 100 kW-class freighters) was found not to close and is abandoned. Design for the
revised architecture below. Do not re-propose the abandoned design.

### Agreed by all three re-assessment models
- Split Phase 0 into 0A (research + pathfinders) and gated 0B (industrial): Structure agreed; budgets → §3 (All three)
- Abandon 50 kt/yr central SEL4/L5 ore processing: — (All three)
- Co-locate at least beneficiation and primary processing at the target NEA; ship product, not ore: Reference architecture (All three. GPT: "favoured but not universally optimal". Claude retains a central station fed with ≥20:1 concentrate as an alternative. Gemini's own weighted QOC scores SEL1 marginally higher (see §6).)
- Narrow product to native/reduced Fe-Ni; defer solar-grade Si and oxide-derived Al/Si: Fe-Ni baseline; Al/Si pilot or deferred (All three)
- Delivered product scale of order 1 kt/yr: 0.6–2.5 kt/yr (Claude 0.6–2.2 (central 1.3); Gemini 1.0–2.5 (1.5, of which 0.3 is water); GPT 0.6–1.0 contracted (0.67–1.33 capacity))
- MW-class cargo tugs: 1.0–2.5 MWe each; 10–18 tugs; 150–300 t payload (→ §3 for point values)
- Robots powered by HV tether from site power, with onboard battery for mobility and safe-mode: 1–3 kV; battery 10–50 kWh (Claude 2–3 kV, 10–30 kWh; Gemini 1–3 kV, 15–25 kWh; GPT 20–50 kWh, voltage unspecified)
- Delete the 200–500 MWh Li-ion line; size storage per site: 0.5–15 MWh total (Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh; Gemini <15 MWh (YAML 10 MWh))
- Reject $5/W array pricing: Hardware ~$30–150/W, launch separately accounted (Claude $30–150/W hardware ($50–230 installed incl. launch); Gemini $60–100/W (spec $75, range $50–110); GPT $30–100/W allowance ($45–220 with delivery))
- Replace 32–50 × 100 kg monoprop prospectors: Remote survey + 4–10 EP rendezvous scouts of 200–600 kg (All three agree a monoprop bus has ~0.5–0.8 km/s Δv. Remote-survey method differs (→ §3).)
- Add an Earth-to-space launch/delivery line: Line agreed; magnitude → §3 (All three)
- Add a comms, ground segment and mission-operations line; DSN not assumed free: Line agreed (All three. Claude and GPT reject the round-1 2.5 TB/day (~230 Mbps) figure.)
- Phase 0 uncrewed; remove habitat and quarterly visits: 0 crew visits (All three. Claude and GPT reject the "human-rating" label in favour of structural reserve plus docking/servicing interfaces. Gemini keeps docking ports and structural margins without commenting on the label.)
- Add an EP propellant supply line; xenon not baselined: Line agreed; demand → §3 (All three)
- No production LOX/LH₂ in Phase 0: — (All three. Claude and GPT remove the EML1 depot; Gemini "defers" cryo depots to 0B/Phase 1.)
- Add NRE, pathfinder, spares and contingency lines: Lines agreed; values → §3 (All three)
- Write a full organization (bom-0-7) specification: ~$100–350M (Claude $100–300M; Gemini $150–250M (text $200M); GPT $150–350M)
- Add a debris/contamination requirement and budget tighter than 99%: $50–300M (Threshold → §3)
- Freeze one configuration-controlled baseline; mark legacy documents superseded: — (All three)
- Earth-supplied material as a fallback if microgravity metallurgy fails: — (All three. Ranking relative to lunar → §3.)
- Tie Phase 0 output to Phase 1 demand with a material/purity/date specification: — (All three)
- Add waste-heat rejection (radiators) explicitly: Item agreed; sizing → §3 (All three)

### Owner decisions
- D-01 (accepted 2026-10-12): Fund 0A. Hold 0B as a gated real option, sized at the gate by signed Phase 1 demand. Call Phase 0 a capability programme, not a cost saving.
- D-02 (accepted 2026-10-12): Hybrid: NASA life-cycle gates with TRL/AD² for each critical technology, plus four discriminating gates (target, demand, economics, licence). Stringency follows reversibility.
- D-03 (proposed; treat as interim): Set an ALARP requirement with an interim design ceiling. The number itself goes to modelling, tests and the licensing state.
- D-04 (proposed; treat as interim): Use SEL1 as the reference case. Re-decide jointly with Phase 1 at the 0B gate.
- D-05 (proposed; treat as interim): Select no propellant yet. Cost iodine as the reference case and argon as the alternate, pending the supply audit and life tests. Water EP stays a desk study until a C-type target is confirmed.

Under D-02, KDP-0B (the one-way commitment to 0B production) needs every project-ending technology
at TRL 6 in a relevant environment with no waivers; internal 0A milestones need TRL 4–5.

### This item: bom-0-5 Site Power, Arrays and Storage (0B)
Accepted scope: Site power generation and HV distribution at the NEA, with distributed storage sized per site. The 200–500 MWh generic battery bank is removed. Whether tug arrays are counted here or with the tugs differs by model; state your choice.

Round-2 proposals for this item (per model; not approved as numbers):
- resize · bom-0-5 site power / arrays · supported by all · quantity: Claude 2.5–8 MW site (tug arrays moved to bom-0-4); Gemini 50 MW; GPT 35–50 MW total · cost: Claude $0.2–1.2B line; Gemini $60–100M per MW; GPT $30–100/W · confidence: low–medium
- add · distributed storage · supported by Claude (within bom-0-5), Gemini, GPT · quantity: Claude 0.5–3 MWh + thermal; Gemini ≤10–15 MWh; GPT 1.3–3.3 MWh · cost: GPT $50–140M/MWh; others not separately priced · confidence: medium (Claude, GPT)
- remove · 200–500 MWh generic battery bank · supported by all · quantity: 0 · cost: — · confidence: medium–high

Critical technologies (TRL re-baseline, panel envelope):
- T02 MW-scale deployable solar arrays (tug; site per Gemini and GPT): TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5, project-ending
- T09 High-voltage power tethers and site distribution on regolith: TRL 2–4 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, architecture-change
- T15 Site power generation and transfer: TRL 2–3 now, target 6, AD² 5–6, project-ending
- T20 Distributed energy storage (GPT: and microgrid power management): TRL 3–5 now, target 6, AD² 4–5, architecture-change

Other Phase 0 items (do not duplicate their scope): bom-0-1 Prospecting Survey and Rendezvous Scouts; bom-0-2 Mining Robots; bom-0-3 Processing Plant at the Target NEA; bom-0-4 MW-class Cargo Tugs; bom-0-6 Water Pilot (C-type target only); bom-0-7 Organizational Infrastructure; bom-0-8 Earth-to-Space Launch and Delivery; bom-0-9 Communications and Ground Segment; bom-0-10 Mission Operations; bom-0-11 NRE, Ground R&D and Qualification; bom-0-12 0A Pathfinder Demonstrator; bom-0-13 Phase 1 Receiving Node (SEL1); bom-0-14 Spares and Replacements; bom-0-15 Debris and Contamination Control; bom-0-16 Electric-Propulsion Propellant Supply; bom-0-17 Contingency and Reserve.

State quantities and costs as ranges with their basis, split 0A and 0B where the item spans both,
and say where you disagree with the round-2 figures and why.

### Round-2 reconciliation for this item

# Reconciliation: bom-0-5 Solar Power Arrays (Phase 0), Round 2

**Panel and attribution.** In this document, **Claude** means Claude Opus 5.5, **Gemini** means Gemini 3.8 Flash and **GPT** means GPT-6.1 Sol. These are the names in the response headers. The `model:` fields in the YAML blocks do not match those headers:

- Gemini's YAML reads `claude-opus-5.5-engineer`.
- GPT's YAML reads `GPT-5.2`.

This reconciliation attributes by response header. The mismatch should be corrected before records are filed (see Reviewer note).

---

## 1. Verdict matrix

| Finding | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| **P0-F03** Station power cannot refine 50 kt/yr | agree | agree | partly |
| **P0-F04** 100 MW with ~5 MW identified load, no site split, storage without night | partly¹ | agree | partly |
| **P0-F05** $5/W far below current prices, excludes launch | agree | agree | agree |

¹ Claude's prose says "agree on site split and storage; partly on '~95 MW has no load'". Its YAML records `partly`.

**Where the panel stands**

- **P0-F03.** All three say a mixed slate that includes reduced Al or Si cannot close at 1–2.5 MW. They split on the finding's absolute wording:
  - Gemini says even pure native-metal melting (~4.4 MW) exceeds 1–2.5 MW.
  - Claude says 1–2.5 MW can melt ~15–40 kt/yr of native metal.
  - GPT says native metal alone needs 1.7–2.9 MW before auxiliaries. On that basis GPT "can approach" the range, so it records `partly`.
- **P0-F04.** All three agree the site split is missing and the 200–500 MWh storage is unjustified at L4/L5. Claude and GPT add that, once F03 is applied, the station absorbs most of the 100 MW. In their view the "~95 MW unassigned" is a documentation and allocation defect, not proof of oversizing. Gemini agrees with the finding without addressing the oversizing question, and also allocates most of the 100 MW to the station.
- **P0-F05.** The panel is unanimous that $5/W is unsupported and that delivery is missing. It is not unanimous on the replacement value.

---

## 2. Agreed changes

These are the changes all three models support. Where they support the direction but differ on numbers, the "consolidated" column gives the **panel span** (lowest to highest value stated) together with each model's central value.

Claude and GPT both warn that a union of model ranges is not an evidence-based uncertainty interval:

- Claude: such a union "hides the fact that a single upstream number dominates every downstream decision".
- GPT: "agreement among models using similar assumptions does not increase the underlying evidence quality".

The spans below should be read in that light.

Per-site values diverge (§3, D2) |
| A3 | Delete the 200–500 MWh bulk storage. Replace it with a small station buffer plus per-site storage. Sites currently have 0 MWh. | 5 MWh station (2–10) + 4 × 0.3 MWh (0.1–0.5) ≈ 6.2 MWh | 15 MWh station + 4 × 3 MWh = 27 MWh (18–40) | 4.3 MWh total (2.4–6.4); station 0.8–2, sites 0.4–1.1 each | Total 4.3–27 MWh; span 2.4–40 MWh |
| A4 | Replace $5/W / $500M. Delivery to destination must be costed somewhere. | $70/W all-in (25–450); $40/W hardware (15–300) | $75/W all-in (45–150 in YAML; 45–160 in prose) | $90–410/W all-in package | All-in central $70–~$200/W; span $25–450/W. All three rate confidence below "high" (Claude low, Gemini medium, GPT low) |
| A5 | Set system specific power | 100 W/kg (60–150) | 110 W/kg (90–135), wing level | 100 W/kg (80–150) | Central 100–110 W/kg; span 60–150 |

GPT and Claude rate confidence low; Gemini medium |
| A8 | Station heat rejection is missing from the BOM and must be carried | 15–35 MW_th (central ~28) | 45–60 MW_th (~55) | 30–60 MW screening | All agree it is missing. Value span 15–60 MW_th (see D10) |
| A9 | NEA site anchoring and dust mitigation is missing scope | Listed | Listed | Listed | Agreed as missing; not costed by any model |

---

## 3. Preserved divergences

### D1. Station power: values and inputs
The three central values differ (A1) because the models use different inputs:

| Input | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fe-Ni melt (kWh/kg) | 0.5–1.5 (c_p ~0.65 kJ/kg·K) | ~0.70 (c_p ~0.45 kJ/kg·K) | 0.5–1.0 |
| MRE Al / Si (kWh/kg) | 15–30 each; floors 8.6 / 9.0 from ΔH | 13–20; floor 6–8 from ΔG | Al 15–25; MG-Si 15–30 |
| Solar-grade upgrade | +40–100 | +25–60 | 45–120 including reduction (30–90 for purification) |
| Operating basis | 85% availability, ×1.56 BOL conversion | 8,000 h/yr | 8,760 h with 85% availability; +4–8 MW auxiliaries |
| Reference slate | Three slates (low / central / high) | 70% Fe-Ni, 20% Al/Fe oxide, 10% Si | 40 kt Fe-Ni, 8 kt Al, 2 kt solar-grade Si |

Each model's stated confidence:
- Claude: station allocation low, "slate-driven".
- GPT: low.
- Gemini: "high" in its YAML, "medium" in its table.

### D2. Total nameplate and NEA allocation

| Position | Models | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| 80 MW BOL total (50–115 central slate; 30–200 across slates). The total is an output of the per-site requirements, not an input. Includes a 10 MW reserve. | Claude | Station 60 + NEA 10 + reserve 10. None of the fixed totals should be adopted before bom-0-3 publishes a slate. |
| 100 MW (85–120), high confidence | Gemini | 75 MW station + 25 MW NEA |
| 100 MW kept only as a "conditional sizing envelope" (80–130), low confidence; "not a procurement authorization" | GPT | 80 MW station + 20 MW NEA. "70 vs 100 MW: not resolvable without the product slate." |

| NEA allocation | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per site, BOL | 2.5 MW (1.8–5), day-only | 6.25 MW | 5 MW |
| Aggregate | 10 MW (8–20) | 25 MW (15–30) | 20 MW (12–24) |
| Design distance | 1.5 AU (notes Amor aphelia >2 AU) | Derated to 3.5 MW EOL at 1.35 AU (range 1.1–1.5 AU) | 1.8 MW EOL at 1.3 AU; 1.3 MW at 1.5 AU |

### D3. ISPP load per site

| Position | Models |
|---|---|
| 0.25 MW as specified (yields ~110–220 t/yr water per unit); ~1 MW if scaled. Water energy 10–13 kWh/kg. | Claude |
| 2.5–3.5 MW per site (10–14 MW aggregate); "BOM undersized ISPP" | Gemini |
| 1 MW running per site (4 MW aggregate), roughly half-time in daylight; 10–25 kWh/kg water; 0.25 MW "not retained as a proven requirement" | GPT |

### D4. Who consumes ISPP H₂/O₂
- Claude says there is no Phase-0 customer, because the tugs burn Kr or iodine. In its view this makes ISPP array power "pure demonstration" and removes most of the value of NEA night operations.
- GPT agrees that H₂/O₂ "need an identified user" and that ISPP output "does not establish compatibility with krypton/iodine tugs".
- Gemini does not address the question.

### D5. Station storage driver and size

| Position | Models | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| 5 MWh (2–10) | Claude | MRE keep-alive at 5–10% of MRE load for 1–2 h. "A frozen electrolyte cell is a likely loss of the cell." Claude says GPT's round-1 station value omitted keep-alive. |
| 15 MWh | Gemini | ~15 min at full load (55 MW). Covers 15–20 min of reorientation or bus-fault clearing "without … solidifying molten electrolyte pots". |
| 0.8–2 MWh | GPT | ~1 h of critical services plus a defined shutdown. GPT caveats that "survival-only backup may be insufficient if molten processes require prolonged controlled cooldown". |

### D6. Battery pack specific energy, and the mass of the original 200–500 MWh

| Position | Models |
|---|---|
| 100–160 Wh/kg pack level, so 500 MWh ≈ 3,100–5,000 t. The finding's 1,000–2,500 t "is a cell-level figure". | Claude |
| 200 Wh/kg pack level, so 1,000–2,500 t | Gemini |
| 80–160 Wh/kg pack level | GPT |

### D7. NEA night operations
- Claude treats night operations as a priced option. It roughly doubles throughput but needs about 2× the array and 2–6 MWh per site.
- Gemini's baseline includes 3 MWh per site for "night-side survival/continuous operations".
- GPT makes daylight-only production its provisional case and calls continuous versus daylight-only "a genuine cost/throughput trade-off".

### D8. Cell technology

| Position | Models | Reasoning |
|---|---|---|
| Technology-neutral, with a must-pass screen of ≥25 MW/yr qualified supply. Choose on delivered EOL $/W. Efficiency 22–32%. | Claude | Claude estimates (low confidence) global space III-V output at "a few MW/yr". It judges 100 MW of III-V "likely infeasible" on a Phase-0 schedule (medium-low confidence; falsifiable by RFI). |
| Qualified III-V baseline (29–32%), silicon alternative permitted, no unqualified tandem baseline | GPT | "Producing 100 MW of qualified space hardware is itself a programme". Notes that a universal 40–60 W/kg limit for silicon is not established. |
| Conditional on launch cost: "III-V wins" if launch-constrained; silicon is competitive below ~$500/kg to LEO. Silicon gives 70–85 W/kg and ~60% lower bare-cell cost. | Gemini | Does not address supply capacity |

### D9. Cost: value and structure

| Element | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hardware $/W | 40 (15–300) | ~30 (volume floor $25–45; heritage $150–400) | 45–170 recurring |
| LEO launch $/kg | Falcon list $1,500–4,000; Starship-class assumed $200–1,000 | "Modern commercial" $1,000–1,500 | Falcon 9 arithmetic ~$3,000 |
| Destination delivery | 1.5–3× LEO $/kg, or SEP self-delivery | $2,500–4,500/kg delivered | $3,000–10,000/kg; "lower end is optimistic" |
| Line total | ~$5.6B all-in for 80 MW; 80% interval $3–20B | $7.5B ($4.5–15B) for 100 MW | $9–41B for 100 MW (YAML central $20B), "scenario envelope, not a statistical confidence interval" |
| Reserve / development | NRE $0.3–1B as a separate line | Not stated | 30% reserve plus $0.5–2B first-of-kind development, inside the envelope |

Explicit cross-critiques:
- Claude judges that GPT's round-1 $100–750/W "treats heritage pricing as baseline". It is unlikely that 100 MW would be bought at heritage prices.
- Claude also says Gemini's round-1 "high confidence" on ~$35/W is "not warranted by any public evidence".
- GPT cites the Boeing iROSA contract ($103M / 120 kW ≈ $860/W) as a reality check. GPT caveats that the contract "is not an array-only quotation".

### D10. Station heat-rejection magnitude and basis

| Position | Models |
|---|---|
| 15–35 MW_th. Credits ~25–30% of input leaving as chemical energy in metal and O₂. Most rejection is at furnace temperature; ~3–4 MW_th at ~330 K (3,000–5,000 m²). | Claude |
| All delivered electrical energy (50–65 MW) "must eventually be rejected"; 55 MW_th at 200–400 K; ">$1.0B scope" | Gemini |
| 30–60 MW screening, "not simply equal to PV output"; a heat and chemical-energy balance is required. 40 MW at 400–500 K needs ~13,000–31,000 m². | GPT |

### D11. Degradation specification
- Claude: 15-year EOL/BOL ≥0.80 (0.72–0.88), with silicon at the low end. Low–medium confidence.
- Gemini: 0.8%/yr (0.6–1.2), "quiet solar wind". Medium confidence.
- GPT: retained-output requirement of 75–85% after 15 years. Must include solar-particle events. Low confidence.

### D12. Phase-0 throughput: fixed or reducible
- Claude says the panel never tested reducing throughput. It proposes options (b) native-metal-only and (c) a 5–10 MW pilot with ~1 kt/yr MRE, as a values question for human reviewers.
- GPT proposes phased throughput and a staged demonstration, and says "accept that the 50 kt/yr target may fall".
- Gemini's options all assume the full 50 kt/yr.

### D13. Meaning of "50 kt/yr"
- Claude raises hypothesis H4: 50 kt may be *feed* tonnage. It flags that feed of 100–500 kt/yr could imply 0.3–6 MW of mining-site beneficiation load.
- GPT: "feed, recovered metal, all solids and oxygen-inclusive output give fundamentally different requirements".
- Gemini assumes 50 kt of mixed product. Its falsification test is a feed with <10% native metal, which would push power above 110 MW.

### D14. NEA site power architecture
- Gemini puts orbital microwave or laser beaming forward as Option B, with 45–55% end-to-end efficiency. It considered fission for the NEAs and rejected it on development and regulatory risk (>$5B).
- GPT: beaming is "not a baseline solution", and its architecture and link efficiency are unproven.
- Claude assumes surface arrays and does not discuss beaming.

### D15. Interface `in_bom` status

| Interface | Claude | Gemini | GPT |
|---|---|---|---|
| bom-0-2 robot power | No | Yes | Yes |
| bom-0-3 station power | No | No | Yes |
| bom-0-6 ISPP power | No | No | Yes |
| bom-0-1 site data | No | — | Yes |

### D16. Location and inter-site distance
- Claude corrects the finding's "tens of millions of km". It puts L4/L5 at ~1 AU (~150 million km) from Earth and at tens to >200 million km from NEA targets. Claude says the consequence (no power transfer) is unchanged.
- Neither Gemini nor GPT comments on this.

### D17. Array self-delivery by SEP
- Claude evaluates arrays powering their own Kr/iodine SEP stage:
  - ~350 t of propellant from LEO, or ~20–60 t from C3 ≈ 0.
  - Krypton supply at that scale is unverified.
- Gemini assumes an electric orbital tug at 3.5–4.5 km/s.
- GPT keeps tug propulsion power onboard the tugs and says transfer propellant is "missing, not zero".

**Status:** these are proposals for human review. None is approved.

**Scope named as missing but not entered as a delta line:**

| Scope | Models and positions |
|---|---|
| HV PMAD and switchgear | Gemini lists as missing; Claude carries it in hardware $/W ("do not add it again"); GPT includes local PMAD but wants station-wide ownership made explicit |
| Anchoring and dust mitigation | All three |

**Double-counting caution.** Claude flags the double-counting risk and resolves it by putting delivery on a separate line. GPT includes delivery, development and reserves inside its package. If the reviewers adopt Claude's B4 or B5 together with GPT's B1 basis, those costs are counted twice.

---

## 5. Open questions

| Question | What would settle it | Raised by |
|---|---|---|
| Product slate in t/yr per product. Does "50 kt/yr" count feed, metal, solids or O₂? | The bom-0-3 author publishes the slate with kWh/kg and an O₂ mass balance | Claude, GPT; Gemini (mineralogical split) |
| Phase-0 objective: production station (~60–80 MW BOL) or 5–10 MW pilot / phased throughput? | A programme values decision | Claude, GPT |
| Practical MRE and solar-grade kWh/kg with representative feed | Sustained pilot including auxiliaries, recovery and purification | Claude (low certainty), GPT (process-energy gate) |
| MRE cell thermal hold time at 5–10% keep-alive | Thermal model or pilot cooldown test | Claude; GPT (shutdown energy) |
| Supplier capacity and price at ≥25 MW/yr | Supplier RFI with $/W, production rate, yield, qualification and warranty | Claude, GPT |

### 3.3 Annual energy and throughput closure

At 1.5 MW scheduled production load and 3,000–4,500 productive hours annually:

\[
E_{\rm production}=4.5\text{–}6.75\ {\rm GWh/year}
\]

For 1,000 t/year of accepted output, this corresponds to:

\[
4.5\text{–}6.75\ {\rm kWh/kg\ of\ accepted\ product}
\]

That is a **whole-site energy envelope**, including beneficiation and auxiliaries—not a proposed metal-melting energy requirement.

Whether this envelope is sufficient depends strongly on native-metal abundance, recovery, feed handling, and product quality. It also does not establish that 1,000 t/year will be delivered: transport losses, inventory, and receiving acceptance remain separate interfaces.

For example:

\[
M_{\rm feed}=\frac{M_{\rm accepted\ product}}{f_{\rm recoverable\ metal}\,\eta_{\rm recovery}}

At 20% recoverable metal and 80% recovery, 1,000 t of product requires approximately 6,250 t of feed. At 2%, it requires approximately 62,500 t. Those cases cannot share an unexamined mining-power assumption.

### 5.1 Voltage selection

Adopt **3 kV DC as the development baseline**.

- Conceptual bipolar reference: ±1.5 kV relative to a controlled electrical reference.
- All insulation must nevertheless tolerate the defined full differential and credible fault/transient voltages.
- Do not use regolith as a return conductor or protective earth.
- Use two-conductor circuits, bonding networks, insulation monitoring, and isolated load converters.

This voltage reduces cable mass without making a jump to substantially higher, less mature operating voltages.

### 5.2 Distribution requirements

| Parameter | Preliminary requirement |

| Primary voltage | 3 kV DC nominal |
| Typical controlled feeder | 250–500 kW |
| Essential low-voltage services | Redundant isolated DC buses; voltage standardized with site equipment |
| Fault protection | Converter current limiting plus independently powered isolation |
| Fault containment | Single branch fault must not disable both essential buses |
| Robot interfaces | Dead-front connectors; interlocked mate/demate |

A representative 500 kW feeder draws 167 A at 3 kV. For a 500 m one-way route using two 70 mm² copper conductors:

- Loop resistance: approximately 0.25 Ω at room temperature.
- Resistive loss: approximately 7 kW.
- Bare copper mass: approximately 0.63 t.

This is an electrical screening calculation, **not a qualified cable design**. Vacuum ampacity, insulation temperature, solar heating, terminations, and fault energy determine the final cross-section.

### 5.3 Arc and stored-energy control

Protection cannot rely on terrestrial breaker assumptions. A local fault can be sustained by batteries and converter capacitors even after array isolation.

Required measures include:

- Segmented source capacitance.
- Precharge and controlled discharge circuits.
- Arc detection and converter shutdown.
- Independent battery contactors.
- Insulation resistance monitoring.
- Voltage-presence indication at service interfaces.
- Verified isolation before robotic handling.
- Fault tests covering solar-wind plasma, dust, and exposed dielectric charging.

Final trip times and let-through energies must follow equipment damage tests, not arbitrary generic thresholds.

\[

## 8. Autonomy, control, and communications

Earth cannot provide real-time electrical protection.

### Control hierarchy

1. **Local protection:** hardware-level overcurrent, arc, insulation, and thermal protection.
2. **Converter control:** voltage regulation, current limiting, MPPT, and battery control.
3. **Site energy management:** forecast-driven scheduling, load admission, and reserve management.
4. **Ground supervision:** planning, anomaly review, software authorization, and performance trending.

### Required autonomous functions

- Black-start one essential bus from any healthy battery unit.
- Recover from a failed controller without losing essential power.
- Reconfigure around a failed array or distribution section.
- Forecast generation from rotation, ephemeris, and terrain horizon maps.
- Admit production batches only if completion/shutdown energy is available.
- Defer charging and production before violating survival reserves.
- Detect declining insulation resistance and quarantine suspect branches.
- Operate safely through communications outages.

Use redundant fiber links for primary site control where practical. Local wireless may support inspection and mobility but must not be the sole protection channel.

Preliminary external telemetry allocation:

- **20–100 kbps average** power-system telemetry.
- Event-triggered waveform records and inspection imagery.
- Local buffering sized for at least 30 days of routine records, with protected retention of critical fault data.

These are interfaces to bom-0-9, not an additional communications system budget.

- Battery units.
- Feeder isolation modules.
- Robotic mechanical and electrical interfaces.
- Inspection targets and diagnostic connections.

Require production acceptance tests for every blanket section, converter channel, battery assembly, and HV termination.

### 9.2 Deployment sequence

1. Survey terrain and verify selected anchor locations.
2. Establish a low-power bootstrap station and communications.
3. Deploy the first stationary battery and essential bus.
4. Deploy and commission one array module.
5. Verify restraint loads, pointing, insulation, and thermal behavior.
6. Expand sequentially, testing each new section before connection.
7. Commission process loads only after both essential buses and required storage are available.
8. Demonstrate autonomous fault recovery before industrial operation.

No human visits are assumed.

### 9.3 Maintainability

The operational servicing unit should be a blanket section, converter, battery assembly, or restraint component—not an entire 500 kW module where avoidable.

Include:

- Accessible standardized fasteners.
- Captive covers and restrained small parts.
- Isolation points visible to robotic inspection.
- No dependence on manual connector cleaning.
- Replaceable sacrificial protection near dusty work zones.
- Installation geometry that permits replacement without crossing energized equipment.

## 11. Development roadmap and technology readiness

The supplied panel envelopes place the critical systems below industrial readiness. Mature cells do not make a complete NEA microgrid mature.

### 11.1 0A development sequence

| Stage | Demonstration | Exit objective |
|---|---|---|
| Laboratory breadboards | HV converters, dust-exposed interfaces, battery controls, representative process-load profiles | TRL 4 |
| Integrated environmental testing | Plasma/vacuum HV tests, deployment tests, thermal cycling, representative anchor and cable trials | TRL 5 |
| Relevant-environment demonstration | Array deployment, local transfer, storage, fault isolation, autonomous operation | Evidence toward TRL 6 |
| Production-representative qualification | Repeated-unit architecture, full-scale critical deployment elements, endurance and fault testing | TRL 6 evidence package |

A **100–250 kW flight demonstrator** can establish important evidence, but does not automatically qualify a 500 kW module. Full-scale critical structures, electrical stresses, fault energies, and scaling laws require separate demonstration.

Prefer a target-body pathfinder that exercises real surface attachment and rotation conditions. Ground facilities can reproduce some plasma and thermal conditions, but not all coupled NEA deployment dynamics.

### 11.2 Technology-specific closure

| Technology | Required evidence |
|---|---|
| **T02: MW-scale deployable arrays** | Production-representative deployment units, stable pointing, output retention, structural dynamics, and a validated repeated-module scaling approach |
| **T09: HV tethers/distribution** | Dust/plasma insulation behavior, cable handling, fault isolation, connector endurance, and robotic servicing |
| **T15: site generation and transfer** | Integrated generation-to-load operation with relevant deployment, attachment, and site dynamics |
| **T20: storage/microgrid management** | Endurance, fault containment, black start, load shedding, reserve enforcement, and validated shutdown energy |

Under D-02, **T02 and T15 must reach TRL 6 with no waivers before KDP-0B**. I also recommend requiring T09 and T20 at TRL 6 for this selected architecture: their failure would otherwise force a late industrial redesign.

Internal 0A milestones remain TRL 4–5.

### 11.3 KDP-0B conditions

In addition to technology readiness:

- **Target:** measured illumination, mineralogy, surface mechanics, and dynamics support the design.
- **Demand:** signed Phase 1 material, purity, quantity, delivery-date, and receiving specifications.
- **Economics:** supplier-backed hardware estimates and closed delivery mass/trajectory model.
- **Licence:** approved contamination, debris, electrical safety, and operations case.

A development schedule should be evidence-driven. As a planning allowance, expect **several years of ground development followed by a multi-year flight demonstration and evaluation campaign**, not immediate industrial deployment.

## 13. Risk assessment

| Risk | Consequence | Primary mitigation / gate |
|---|---|---|
| Illumination worse than assumed | Throughput collapse or excessive storage | Terrain-resolved annual illumination model before target selection |
| Anchoring or deployment failure | Loss of expensive array modules; debris | Relevant-environment demonstration; independent modules |
| HV arcing in plasma/dust | Bus outage, erosion, fire-like thermal damage | Segmentation, qualified insulation, fault-energy testing |
| Feed grade or recovery poorer than assumed | Excess mining energy per accepted kilogram | Integrated feed-to-product pilot and target rejection criteria |
| Process shutdown energy underestimated | Battery depletion or plant damage | Measured shutdown tests before final storage sizing |
| Supplier capacity insufficient | Schedule slip and cost escalation | Capacity audit and production-representative contracts |
| Array pointing excites structural dynamics | Reduced output, anchor overload | Coupled flexible-body/attitude model and flight validation |
| Battery internal failure | Loss of reserve or propagation | Geographical separation, isolation, containment |
| Dust accumulation and excavation ejecta | PV degradation and radiator damage | Stand-off distance, source control, contamination budget |
| Delivery mass grows | Transport cost and schedule failure | Packing, trajectory, and deployment closure before procurement |
| Autonomous load management fails | Unstable bus or reserve exhaustion | Hardware-in-the-loop fault campaigns; independent reserve protection |
| Demand changes | Stranded industrial capacity | Modular procurement tied to signed Phase 1 demand |

For debris and contamination, follow the interim **ALARP** approach. Do not invent a “safe” release fraction. Model credible deployment, excavation, cable, and array-fragment release mechanisms and establish acceptance limits with the licensing state.

## 14. Where this proposal disagrees with Round 2

### 14.1 Reject 35–100 MW site totals as the revised baseline

Those figures largely retain power demands from the abandoned high-throughput mixed-product architecture or aggregate site and tug requirements.

They do not follow from a one-site, order-1-kt/year native/reduced Fe-Ni capability programme.

**My reference is 8 MW at 1 AU BOL, delivering approximately 2.5 MW at 1.5 AU EOL in sunlight.** Larger systems require a demonstrated load and demand case.

### 14.2 Accept the smaller site scale, but clarify its rating

Claude’s revised 2.5–8 MW site range is directionally closest to this proposal. However, “site MW” is ambiguous unless it distinguishes:

- BOL/1 AU array rating;
- EOL output at target distance;
- delivered bus power;
- and annual energy after darkness.

This proposal makes those distinctions explicit.

### 14.3 Storage should stay near 1–3 MWh unless measured loads justify more

The 10–15 MWh proposals are not impossible, but they are not justified by the current reference operating policy. Full-power night production is deliberately excluded.

The 2 MWh reference is supported by a stated emergency budget, with target-specific verification still required.

### 14.4 Reject $5/W, but do not treat $30–150/W as proven

The supplied hardware allowance is suitable for scenario planning, not a procurement commitment. Heritage flight contracts also cannot be scaled mechanically into a definitive industrial price.

### 14.5 Do not carry obsolete process radiator quantities

Radiator sizing must follow the revised heat balance. Neither PV nameplate nor abandoned mixed-product plant power determines site radiator duty.

## Final recommendation

**Develop a modular 8 MW-reference / 2 MWh NEA microgrid in 0A, but purchase industrial capacity only after the target, demand, economics, licence, and TRL gates close.**

The central design principle is simple: **use sunlight to make product, and storage to keep the site safe.** Do not spend launch mass and capital forcing an unproven first industrial site to behave like a continuously powered terrestrial factory.
